name: Gao
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1926. A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages. Cambridge: CUP, pp. 525-538 (Ysabel languages incl. Gao/'Nggao').
new_statements.check: reported by the second reader, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both works are marked silent, so both were spot-checked (files reopened, stress terms searched, fresh downloads attempted). Nothing missed: Ray 1926 pp. 529-532 has no accent line (re-read in full), the HTRC token bags carry no stress-family token on pp. 522-540, the search-inside index has no Ysabel accent/stress snippet, and Capell AC2-SIBUG201 is a bare word list. The only unread text remains Ray pp. 525-528 and 533-538 behind HathiTrust's 403 (four attempts in total now, two mine); the token bags for those pages show no accent/stress/syllable/tone token, so a missed statement there is very unlikely but not directly excluded. New files saved: readall_check_hathi_ray1926_plaintext_seq555/…

sources.citation: Boswell, Fredrick A. 2018. A Grammar of Cheke Holo. LOT Dissertation Series 518. Utrecht: LOT (Leiden University PhD).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Describes Cheke Holo (chek1238), not Gao: sec. 2.9.1 p. 35 'Regardless of word class, the stress on the word root is regularly on the penultimate syllable'. Gao is mentioned only as a neighbouring region/language and via Codrington 1885 (sec. 1.7, p. 11: Codrington's survey 'for Isabel focused on Bughotu and Gao'); no Gao stress statement and no Gao source cited beyond Codrington.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Gao language' (wikitext, accessed 2026-09-17), pointing to PARADISEC collections AC1 (Capell recordings in Gao) and AC2 (Capell field notes on Gao vocabulary).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Stub; no linguistic content. PARADISEC catalogue pages for AC1/AC2 returned an automated-access block by automated download (not accessible), as did Ethnologue (not reachable by automated download), OLAC/language-archives.org (connection refused), sil.org, HathiTrust full-text, endangeredlanguages.com and LSE eTheses (Whiteley).

sources.citation: Voica, Radu. 2017. A Fieldwork-Based Approach to Blanga (Blablanga), an Austronesian Language of the Solomon Islands, with Reference to Predicate-Argument Relations. PhD thesis, SOAS University of London. p. 55.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Gao stress; bibliographic statement only: 'The first description of an Isabel language consists of a five-page grammatical sketch of Gao published by Codrington (1885: 555-559) but except for wordlists and mentions in more general or comparative studies, nothing else has been published to my knowledge.' (p. 55)

sources.citation: White, Geoffrey M., Francis Kokhonigita & Hugo Pulomana. 1988. Cheke Holo (Maringe/Hograno) Dictionary. Pacific Linguistics C-97. Canberra: ANU. Introduction pp. vii-ix.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Gao stress. Treats Gao as a fourth distinct Isabel language (Whiteman & Simons 1978 grouping: (1) Bughotu; (2) Gao; (3) Cheke Holo-Blablanga-Zazao; (4) Zazao-Kokota-Zabana) sharing high cognate percentages with Cheke Holo; lexicon marks some entries '(Gao)'. Cites Whiteman & Simons 1978 MS survey.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B. D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands Languages: An Internal Classification. Pacific Linguistics C-72. Canberra: ANU. (Nggao = wordlist 23; Poro = list 40)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Phonological classification and wordlists; no stress marks and no stress statement for Nggao/Poro (only 4 'stress' hits in the whole text, all prose 'it is stressed that..' or general sound-change notes).

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1926. A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages. Cambridge: CUP, pp. 525-538 (Ysabel languages incl. Gao/'Nggao').
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number 2234.7.25); the open copy could not be downloaded when a reader tried
sources.note: Expands Codrington's Isabel notes to ten 'dialects' (White 1988: vii); Ray sometimes adds accent remarks. HathiTrust full view exists (records 006195824 / 001232162) but page endpoints could not be reached by automated download; archive.org copy access-restricted.

sources.citation: Codrington, Robert H. 1885. The Melanesian Languages. Oxford: Clarendon Press. Section 33 'Ysabel, Gao', pp. 555-559.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The five-page sketch (obtained 'from the first single scholar who came to Norfolk Island from Gao, through a Bugotu interpreter') has an 'Alphabet' section on consonants (kl/gl clusters, loss of g/k, z for Bugotu th) but nothing on accent or stress. The only accent lines in the Ysabel/Florida chapters are for Florida ('The accent of words is generally on the penultimate syllable', p. ~523) and Bugotu ('throwing the accent backwards to the antepenultimate, though by no means as a rule', p. ~542) - not Gao.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. PARADISEC collection AC2 'Field notes' (items on Gao vocabulary, Santa Isabel) and AC1 (audio recordings in Gao).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The only known primary field material on Gao besides Codrington; Capell's notebooks usually mark stress/accent in transcriptions. Catalogue pages were could not be reached by automated download.

sources.citation: Palmer, Bill. 2009. Kokota Grammar. Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 35. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Palmer is the most active Isabel linguist (Boswell 2018: 11) and his Kokota grammar surveys the Isabel subgroup; may contain comparative remarks on Gao prosody. Paywalled (De Gruyter/UHP).

sources.citation: Whiteman, Darrell L. & Gary F. Simons. 1978. The languages of Santa Isabel, Solomon Islands: a sociolinguistic survey. MS, Cornell Working Papers (Language Variation and Limits to Communication Project 4).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only modern Gao-specific linguistic survey (intelligibility/lexicostatistics); Simons' survey reports sometimes include brief phonology notes. Not located online.

sources.note: Glottolog lists no descriptive work for Gao beyond Codrington 1885 (listed by Glottolog as a minimal description), Ray 1897 (New Georgia vocabulary, minimal), Tryon & Hackman 1983 and overview/comparative entries (Ross 2010, ELCat 2022, Whiteley 2014 p.c.).
